summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics: tokens/sec per dollar, caching savings from prefix reuse, and batching tradeoffs. Redwood presented updated cost model and preliminary benchmark numbers; customer asked for a longer benchmark and clarified traffic patterns. Action items assigned for updated spreadsheet, benchmark run, and security follow-up.
topics: Overview of last week's benchmark numbers
Caching / KV-prefix savings and hit rates
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Lena Ruiz: Hi, Lena here.
[00:10] Ravi Menon: Ravi on infra.
[00:12] Priya Shah: Priya from product.
[00:15] Omar Patel: Omar from Redwood, running the bench pieces.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Awesome. Agenda is cost/unit econ review — tokens per second per dollar, caching savings, and batching tradeoffs. We'll walk through the updated sheet, then go over the new numbers from last week's runs.
[00:30] Omar Patel: Quick note, numbers are coming off our v2 quantized build; as a reminder quantization and kernel selection changed token throughput by about 18% vs the unquantized baseline in our lab env, your on-prem might differ.
[00:42] Ravi Menon: When you say 18% is that tokens/sec at 2k sequence? Our traffic is often 512 with long tails to 8k.
[00:49] Omar Patel: Good question — the 18% was measured at average sequence length 1024. For shorter sequences the relative gain shrinks; longer sequences benefit more from KV cache reuse.
[01:05] Lena Ruiz: Can we jump to the sheet? Priya, you sent it earlier?
[01:10] Priya Shah: Yep sending now in the chat — link: drive.google.com/quantaco-poc-costs (note: placeholder link).
[01:16] Maya Chen: Thanks. So first row is baseline hosted api numbers we ran last Wednesday: 3.2k tokens/sec per GPU and estimated $0.45 per 1M tokens using Redwood hosted pricing assumptions and our reserved capacity model.
[01:30] Priya Shah: That $0.45 includes prefix caching savings?
[01:33] Omar Patel: The initial number was raw token cost w/o caching. We also have a separate calc for cached prefixes — if you hit a cached prefix we saw 60-72% CPU/GPU cycles saved for request processing depending on kv hit rate.
[01:45] Ravi Menon: 60-72% sounds high — is that end-to-end or just token generation compute? We care about end-to-end latency and cost including pre/post processing.
[01:53] Omar Patel: That's compute on the generation path (the model inference tokens). End-to-end you should expect 45-60% lower cost per request if your prefix hit rate is in the 40-60% range and your preprocessing is relatively cheap. Our sheet models a conservative 40% cache hit for your FAQ and chat roots.
[02:12] Lena Ruiz: Our current logs show about 35% exact prefix reuse for the FAQ flow and another 15% near-match reuse if we allow normalized matching. How sensitive are the savings to hit rate?
[02:21] Omar Patel: Very sensitive — we included a sensitivity table. At 20% hit rate you see maybe 15-20% cost savings; at 60% you get 45-50% cost savings. The non-linear part comes from batching and amortizing KV overhead.
[02:36] Maya Chen: I'll highlight that on the sheet. Next section is batching tradeoffs. Omar, you tuned batch sizes 16, 32, 64 on the dedicated nodes?
[02:44] Omar Patel: Correct. For your workload we saw tokens/sec increase roughly linearly up to batch 32; at 64 the throughput improved another 12% but p99 latency jumped ~220ms on tail requests. Tradeoff: higher throughput per GPU, but single-request latency suffers.
[03:02] Priya Shah: Our SLA for interactive assistant is 400ms p95 target. p99 can be looser but we don't want it above 2s often. Is the 220ms tail increase pushing p95?
[03:11] Omar Patel: For batch 64 we saw p95 still ~640ms because most requests are short; p99 is where batch effects show. So if p95 is your gating metric, batch 32 looked safe in our env with reserved throughput and modest batching.
[03:27] Ravi Menon: Does Redwood support dynamic batching across routes? We have high variance across routes so we want per-route batch configs.
[03:33] Omar Patel: Yes — per-route batching plus priority queues. You can set soft limits per route and override for high-priority low-latency paths. That's in the rollout config.
[03:41] Lena Ruiz: On the tokens/sec/$ calc — are you amortizing the occupancy and reserved capacity costs? If we buy dedicated, our effective $/token changes with commit level.
[03:50] Maya Chen: Good point. The sheet includes three scenarios: hosted pay-as-you-go, dedicated reserved with 50% commit, and dedicated heavy commit (75%). Each has different unit economics factoring in idle occupancy.
[04:05] Priya Shah: At what commit level do you recommend for Quantaco initial production? We're targeting 300 qps baseline with 50 qps peaks spiky bursts to 1k.
[04:14] Omar Patel: For that pattern, we usually recommend an initial 50% commit with burst capacity enabled. It gives reasonable cost predictability and handles bursts via burst pool without overcommitting.
[04:26] Ravi Menon: How about autoscaling time? If a burst hits, how quickly will Redwood spin up extra capacity in dedicated?
[04:32] Omar Patel: Scale rules can be tuned; cold starts for GPU spin up depends on your infra mode — in our managed Dedicated it's about 3-7 minutes to attach new nodes. For faster response you can provision a warm buffer or use hosted for burst overflow which switches in under 30s via smart routing.
[04:50] Lena Ruiz: That smart routing to hosted sounds interesting — what about data residency and our pre-prod regs?
[04:55] Maya Chen: Routing respects deployment policies; you can restrict specific routes to only Dedicated within your VPC. Burst-to-hosted is opt-in per route and only for non-sensitive routes.
[05:06] Priya Shah: Great. Back to caching — Omar, you mentioned prefix normalization. If we allow normalized matching, what's the false-positive risk and how do we mitigate hallucinations or stale context?
[05:16] Omar Patel: Normalization uses token-level heuristics and L1 similarity; false hits are rare but we provide TTLs and versioned cache keys. If the model or prompt template changes we bump the key version to invalidate old cached prefixes. We also log cache hits for audit.
[05:30] Ravi Menon: That logging — is it retained in audit logs or part of model traces? We need to feed that into Splunk/SIEM.
[05:36] Omar Patel: Audit logs include hit/miss events with key hash, route id, and latency. Those can be shipped to your SIEM via our log exporter.
[05:43] Maya Chen: Omar, can you walk us through the benchmark numbers from last Thursday?
[05:47] Omar Patel: Sure. Slide 2 of the pdf: baseline un-cached 3.2k tokens/sec per GPU; quantized v2 bumped to 3.78k tokens/sec. With a simulated 40% cache hit we saw effective tokens/sec per dollar improve to about 4.9k tokens/sec equivalent since cached requests cost much less.
[06:05] Priya Shah: How are you defining effective tokens/sec? Is it weighted by cost per request?
[06:09] Omar Patel: Yes — effective tokens/sec is total tokens served divided by total GPU-seconds weighted by cost; it's a blended metric to compare different cache and batching setups.
[06:19] Lena Ruiz: Any end-to-end latency numbers for that run?
[06:22] Omar Patel: Tail p95 was 580ms on batch 32 with the quantized model; p99 was 1.8s in that run because we injected some long sequences. Without injection p99 drops to ~1.2s.
[06:34] Ravi Menon: That's OK for async flows, but for chat UX we want p95 under 500ms ideally. Can we shave another 80ms?
[06:40] Omar Patel: You can: smaller batch (16), pre-warm KV cache for hot prefixes, or use a slightly higher throughput model pinned to lower batch size. There's a tradeoff: smaller batch reduces tokens/sec per GPU so cost increases.
[06:52] Maya Chen: I'll add a scenario to the sheet that shows p95 vs $/M tokens across batch sizes 16/32/64 for your traffic.
[06:59] Priya Shah: Regarding cost assumptions — the sheet shows $/GPU-hour at $6.5. What's that number based on?
[07:05] Omar Patel: That's our internal example for a T4-like amortized cost in hosted; dedicated reserved pricing can be lower once you commit. We'll put a sensitivity table in the sheet for $4.5 to $8.5.
[07:16] Lena Ruiz: For our finance team we need a conservative scenario (higher $/hour, lower cache hits). Could you produce a conservative vs base vs optimistic tab?
[07:24] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include conservative/base/optimistic. Maya (laughs) — I mean, we'll include three tabs.
[07:30] Priya Shah: Any notes on quantization compatibility with our model fine-tune? We had some accuracy drop once we quantized earlier.
[07:36] Omar Patel: We run a QA sweep — quantization-aware calibration plus small LL calibration reduces regressions. In your prior POC we saw a 0.6 BLEU-equivalent drop on eval set with naive 8-bit; with per-channel quant and calibration that drop went to 0.15 which is within tolerance. We can run an eval against your holdout to confirm.
[07:56] Ravi Menon: Put that as an action: run eval post-quantization on our holdout.
[07:59] Maya Chen: Noted.
[08:02] Lena Ruiz: Can you also capture the instructions for batch shaping? Our traffic has many tiny requests; naive batching will hold them.
[08:10] Omar Patel: Absolutely — dynamic batch shaping based on request age and priority; we can set max wait time e.g., 10ms for low-latency routes. We'll include suggested defaults for your traffic.
[08:22] Priya Shah: One other ask — we'd like an estimate of tokens/sec/$ for embeddings vs generation since we plan to mix both workloads.
[08:29] Omar Patel: Embeddings are cheaper per token typically because model architecture is smaller; we'll add a comparative table and separate per-route economics.
[08:36] Maya Chen: Ok we're at the midpoint. Any blockers from Quantaco side?
[08:40] Ravi Menon: Two things: we need SOC2 artifacts and a sample KMS integration doc before we move to dedicated, and we want to run a longer realistic traffic benchmark to confirm caching wins.
[08:49] Maya Chen: We'll share SOC2 package — action for Maya; Omar will run the longer benchmark.
[08:53] Priya Shah: For the benchmark, can you simulate our TTLs and normalization rules? If you approximate traffic incorrectly the cache numbers will be off.
[08:59] Omar Patel: We'll ingest your traffic profile — Ravi, could you drop a sample 24h token distribution in the shared folder?
[09:05] Ravi Menon: I'll pull a sanitized slice and upload today.
[09:07] Omar Patel: Great. We'll run a 2-hour replay with 24h-ish distribution and include cache normalization on/off scenarios.
[09:15] Lena Ruiz: For expectations, what's a realistic cache hit improvement if we enable normalization? We track different utterance variants that map to the same canonical intent.
[09:23] Omar Patel: From our experience, normalization plus fuzzy matching can bump hit rates 10-18 points for FAQ style flows. For generative chat it depends more on templating.
[09:33] Maya Chen: Quick interruption — customer question in chat about whether Redwood supports HSM-backed KMS for Private. Ravi is that relevant?
[09:40] Ravi Menon: Yes, we require HSM remote key material for production.
[09:44] Omar Patel: Redwood Private supports BYOK with HSM integrations; we'll share the KMS arch doc.
[09:50] Priya Shah: Perfect.
[09:54] Maya Chen: We'll move on to pricing scenarios. Slide 5 has three charts; Omar can you summarize the conservative tab?
[10:01] Omar Patel: Conservative assumes $8.5 GPU-hour, 20% cache hit, batch 16 default — results show $0.72 per 1M tokens. Base: $0.45 at 40% hit, batch32; optimistic $0.29 at 60% hit and heavy commit.
[10:16] Lena Ruiz: Finance will want the waterfall detail — compute, storage, logging, egress where relevant.
[10:22] Maya Chen: We'll break down the waterfall in the next update.
[10:25] Priya Shah: On devops — how does Redwood instrument cost per route? We want token-level cost attribution in our dashboards.
[10:32] Omar Patel: We provide per-route token accounting and cost buckets exportable to your billing system; you can tag routes and get monthly rollups.
[10:38] Ravi Menon: Do you attach model version tags in traces? We need to do regression analysis post-rollout.
[10:42] Omar Patel: Yes — model version, kernel selection, quantization profile are included in traces.
[10:47] Lena Ruiz: Ok, I'm convinced. Next steps then: get the longer benchmark and a conservative cost tab. Also share SOC2 and KMS docs.
[10:56] Maya Chen: I'll recap real quick.
[10:58] Maya Chen: Items — Maya send updated cost model and SOC2/KMS docs; Omar run 2-hour realistic benchmark and share results; Ravi upload sanitized traffic profile; Lena confirm success criteria; all to sync next Friday same time. Anything else?
[11:12] Priya Shah: Can we also get the batch shaping defaults and recommended per-route configs?
[11:17] Omar Patel: Will include that in the benchmark report.
[11:20] Lena Ruiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:23] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up.
[45:30] Meeting end — call disconnected. Note: transcript may have minor transcription errors; some proper nouns might be off in auto-generated text.
